item.title: After US Democrats' midterm win, Taiwan authorities scramble for cracks in new Congress' door: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-06 23:53:00
Illustration: Liu Rui/GT The DPP authorities fancy that their intensive networking and hedging of bets following the US midterm elections demonstrate sophisticated "political wisdom." Little do they realize that such behavior is not only laughable but also extremely dangerous in the arena of international politics. Such shortsighted political maneuvering can do nothing to change the fate of the DPP authorities as a mere pawn. The US midterm elections have barely concluded, yet some on the island of Taiwan are already anxious. Within just a few days, think tanks and "external affairs" institutions in Taipei sprang into action, organizing one seminar and media interview after another. Green camp politicians and so-called "strategic scholars" rushed to assess the shifting balance of power in the new US Congress, calculating how to establish ties with the incoming powerbrokers in both the House and the Senate as quickly as possible. They are eager to submit their political "pledges of allegiance" through various lobbying channels, even if all they can secure is an empty promise of "support for Taiwan." This kind of restless anxiety - both fearful and impatient - is less a sign of so-called "agile response in external strategy" than a full exposure of the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities' deeply opportunistic and politically parasitic nature. This kind of restlessness fully exposes the true nature of certain politicians on the island as "political chameleons." In the political vocabulary of the DPP authorities, there are no inviolable principles, let alone any steadfast convictions. All they represent is nothing but naked opportunism. Whenever the political winds shift in Washington, these self-proclaimed far-sighted strategists are quick to change course and switch their positions. They know how to play both sides of the aisle and pull strings across the US political spectrum. When the Democrats are in power, they talk about "progressive values," "green transition" and "human rights alliances." When Republicans take control, they overnight adopt a "hardline anti-China posture" and present themselves as staunch advocates of "fully preparing for war." No sooner had the midterm elections concluded than think tanks on the island rushed to compile profiles of newly elected members of the House and the Senate, scheming to redesign their lobbying strategies. In their eyes, regardless of Washington's political ideology or policy agenda, as long as it can provide a fig leaf for the DPP's "Taiwan independence" separatist fantasies, they are willing to bend over backwards to please their American patrons, with little regard for their own dignity. DPP politicians constantly proclaim that "the relations between the US and the Taiwan region are rock-solid" and that the two sides "share democratic values." Yet beneath this polished rhetoric lies a sordid record of naked self-interest. In their dealings with Washington, the DPP authorities go out of their way to flatter their American patrons, willingly putting the foundation of industries vital to the livelihoods of Taiwan residents on the negotiating table. They have effectively handed over Taiwan region's core semiconductor assets as a package, allowing them to be relocated overseas and gradually hollowing out the island's industrial base. Meanwhile, they are also signing off on massive purchases of obsolete military equipment at exorbitant prices, with delivery dates nowhere in sight, squandering Taiwan regional taxpayers' money on Washington's lobbying and military-industrial interest groups. Behind the scenes, their every calculation is driven by the DPP's dream of "staying in power." They seem to imagine that a few cheap declarations of loyalty will bind the US firmly onto their narrow and dangerous "anti-China" bandwagon, while harboring ulterior motives to shirk responsibility and shift the blame whenever Washington actually demands that they pay the price. Such shortsighted political maneuvering can do nothing to change the fate of the DPP authorities as a mere pawn. How can a political party willing to sell out national dignity and cultural roots possibly possess political foresight? The DPP authorities fancy that their intensive networking and hedging of bets following the US midterm elections demonstrate sophisticated "political wisdom." Little do they realize that such behavior is not only laughable but also extremely dangerous in the arena of international politics. Politics requires principles, and international engagement demands credibility. The DPP authorities lack any strategic resolve in their external dealings, while on the island, they know only how to foment confrontation and division. Every frantic maneuver and attempt to test the waters in response to shifts in American political power will not alter in the slightest the historical trend that both sides of the Taiwan Straits belong to one China and that China will inevitably achieve reunification. Instead, they are pushing Taiwan region, step by step, toward an abyss of irreversible disaster. When a pawn becomes so absorbed in its role that it imagines it can dictate the course of the game, the stage is often set for being ruthlessly abandoned. In the harsh reality of great-power competition, history has long established the ultimate fate of opportunists who lack the backing of real strength, have abandoned political integrity, and survive entirely through delusional dependence on others. The more the DPP authorities display their almost neurotic anxiety and fickleness, the more they expose their profound sense of insecurity. The world can clearly see through this desperate political farce unfolding on the island. No matter how frequently seminars are held in Taiwan, or how meticulously DPP lobbyists prepare their briefing materials, none of it can conceal their despicable nature as self-serving opportunists who sacrifice principles for personal gain. The tide of history cannot be stopped by a handful of power-hungry politicians. In the face of the Chinese nation's determined march toward great rejuvenation, all the frantic maneuvers and delusional dreams of those who seek "'Taiwan independence' by relying on the US" and sell themselves out for personal gain will ultimately be crushed beneath the relentlessly advancing wheels of history.

item.title: China adopts cross-border anti-corruption law, a governance milestone with global insights: experts
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-06 23:32:00
This photo taken on March 12, 2026 shows the Great Hall of the People ahead of the closing meeting of the fourth session of the 14th National People's Congress (NPC) in Beijing, capital of China. (Xinhua) China's top legislature on Friday adopted a law to combat cross-border corruption at a legislative session of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress. The law, which takes effect upon promulgation, provides strong legal support for investigating cross-border corruption cases, the Xinhua News Agency reported. The law aims to prevent and punish cross-border corruption, deepen international anti-corruption cooperation, safeguard China's sovereignty, security and development interests, and promote the building of a fair and equitable global anti-corruption governance system, per Xinhua. Chinese analysts said that this law is not only a milestone in advancing the modernization of China's anti-corruption governance system and governance capacity, but also contributes Chinese solutions to the global fight against cross-border corruption. Filling gaps with Chinese solutions Containing 47 articles in six chapters, the law covers mechanisms and responsibilities, case handling and international cooperation, integrity and compliance, and legal liability, among other areas. The law states that efforts to combat cross-border corruption should leave no area beyond oversight, leave no ground uncovered and show zero tolerance for corruption. It also stipulates that such efforts must be conducted in strict accordance with the Constitution and laws, follow statutory procedures, and respect and protect human rights. Integrating prevention, enforcement and countermeasure functions, this law represents a major legislative achievement aligning domestic and foreign-related rule of law and fills the gap in specialized cross-border anti-corruption legislation, Huo Zhengxin, a professor at the China University of Political Science and Law, told the Global Times on Friday. As corruption takes on growing cross-border and foreign-related features, Huo said this law arrives in good time to address new demands and emerging anti-corruption challenges. The law says efforts against cross-border corruption should provide equal protection for the legitimate rights and interests of all types of business entities, uphold order in cross-border business activities, and foster a world-class business environment aligned with market principles, the rule of law and international standards. During its second reading, the draft law requires Chinese companies operating across borders to set up integrity and compliance departments or appoint dedicated staff, based on their size, business scope and risk prevention and control. An article in the Legal Daily noted that defining integrity and compliance duties for cross-border operators guides Chinese outbound enterprises to conduct lawful, compliant and clean operations. Integrity can thus become a core competitive edge, supporting the development of a cordial and clean government-business relationship and a fair global business environment, according to the report. While conveying the Communist Party of China (CPC)'s resolve and will on anti-corruption to the international community, the law sends a warning that corrupt fugitives will be tracked down and held legally accountable wherever they flee, Zhang Xixian, a professor at the Party School of the CPC Central Committee, told the Global Times. It also offers Chinese solutions for global cross-border anti-corruption governance, providing a reference for countries to work together through international collaboration to stop corrupt fugitives from evading punishment overseas and jointly tackle corruption challenges, he added. An unwavering pursuit China has steadily pushed forward its anti-corruption campaign in recent years. At the fifth plenary session of the 20th CPC Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI), held in January, the disciplinary body of the CPC called for reinforced anti-corruption efforts during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-30), Xinhua reported. At the recently concluded fifth plenary session of the 20th Central Committee of the CPC, four areas of focus for steadfastly following a distinctive Chinese path to combating corruption were adopted in a resolution. The four areas are: maintaining a tough stance against corruption, strengthening checks on and oversight over the exercise of power, fortifying the cultural-ethical foundations for championing integrity and disdaining corruption, and enhancing coordinated efforts to prevent corruption by rooting out audacity, opportunity, and desire. In the first half of 2026, China's disciplinary inspection and supervision authorities filed 538,000 cases and imposed sanctions on 412,000 people, including 74 officials at or above the provincial-ministerial level, Xinhua reported. The country has stepped up international cooperation in combating corruption in recent years. In 2025, China deepened international anti-corruption cooperation and investigated 505 cross-border corruption cases. A total of 963 fugitives were repatriated to the country in 2025, per Xinhua. In July of that year, Liang Jinwen, one of China's most wanted graft fugitives, returned to China and turned himself in after 28 years at large overseas. Born in February 1954, Liang was formerly a general manager of an automobile brake company in Zhuhai, South China's Guangdong Province. He was suspected of seizing property by taking advantage of his position before fleeing abroad in November 1996. Since the launch of Operation Sky Net in 2015, China had brought back 14,048 fugitives from more than 120 countries and regions and recovered 66.62 billion yuan ($9.92 billion) in illicit assets by the end of 2024, according to official data.

item.title: Record number of 40 US agricultural firms display at CIIE as Chinese expert urges Washington to deliver on tariff cuts for two-way trade
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-06 23:24:00
View of the booth of California Wine Institute at the American Food and Agriculture Pavilion at the ninth China International Import Expo in Shanghai on November 6, 2026. Photo: Ma Jingjing/Global Times A record number of more than 40 US food and agricultural trade associations and companies attended the 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE) in Shanghai, showcasing a wide range of products from soybeans and wine to poultry and ginseng as they seek to maintain their long relationship with Chinese partners and further explore the vast Chinese market following the recent meeting between the heads of state of the US and China. Early at 9 am on Friday, the American Food & Agriculture Pavilion at the CIIE held a launch ceremony, with various US exhibitors offering tastings of flaxseed butter, nuts and wine from California, and Wisconsin ginseng water to the audience. At the US Soybean Export Council booth, a soybean-shaped mascot greeted the audience, while staff warmly offered free gifts to those who had come to taste soybean-made products. At the start of the ceremony, several people in cowboy outfits sang Take Me Home, Country Road . The whole scene brought to life the down-to-earth and welcoming character of US farmers in one of their most important markets. Active participation Spanning 400 square meters, the American Food & Agriculture Pavilion brought together a record number of more than 40 trade associations and companies this year, compared with 19 exhibitors at the 8th CIIE last year. US exhibitors closed six deals worth more than $650 million at the Pavilion's signing ceremony on Friday. The largest came from Illinois-based Hang Tung Resources, which closed three deals for sorghum and wheat worth about $600 million. Other highlights included $51 million in beef sales by New York-based CLB Management and a $1.5 million contract signed by Idaho-based animal nutrition company Dynamite, according to a press release the American Chamber of Commerce in Shanghai sent to the Global Times. "This year's record turnout speaks for itself, as does the scale of the deals signed on the first day," said AmCham Shanghai President Eric Zheng. "American food and agriculture companies see real opportunity in the Chinese market. Practical business cooperation like this is what strengthens ties between our two countries, and it is how we get to a constructive relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity," Zheng said. Brady Holst is a US farmer and vice chairman of the Illinois Soybean Association. It is the first time for him to come to China, and his first time attending the CIIE. "We have spent a lot of time and years developing relationships with different buyers and people in China. They are good partners and friends. When they buy our soybeans, they know someone is actually growing them for them. This personal connection between a farmer and a buyer is what has been very positive," Holst told the Global Times at the expo on Friday. He said that he expects to meet more people who are interested in buying US agricultural products, growing that relationship and friendship between the two countries and farmers and buyers. Holst's wish, in many ways, reflects a much bigger picture. Agricultural trade remains an important component of the China-US economic and trade relationship, and has drawn a great deal of attention following the recent meeting between the two countries' heads of state. Pragmatism urged from Washington China has always been open to expanding its purchases of agricultural products from the US, but with the precondition that the two sides' arrangement for a $30 billion reciprocal tariff reduction is implemented, a spokesperson with China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) said on Thursday. Huang Ling, the MOFCOM spokesperson, expressed the hope that the US side can work with China to create more favorable conditions for agricultural trade between the two countries by jointly reducing tariffs, cutting non-tariff barriers and expanding market access. Maintaining the stable development of China-US economic and trade relations serves the interests of both countries and peoples, and is also beneficial for global economic development. The two sides should meet each other halfway, adhere to the principle of mutual benefit and win-win results, and promote the sustained, stable and sound development of China-US economic and trade relations, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Friday. China and the US held the eighth round of their economic and trade consultations in New York and Washington, DC in September. In the consultations, the two sides agreed to reduce tariffs on about $30 billion worth of goods imported from each other on a reciprocal basis, with tariffs on around 90 percent of the covered products to be lowered to most-favored-nation rates. These reductions will be implemented simultaneously after each side completes domestic legal procedures. Earlier media reports suggested that many US farmers have experienced a hard time over the past several years due to the US administration's tariffs and other multiple factors. According to a Reuters report in February 2026, former US agriculture officials and top Republican senators warned that US farmers were suffering heavy losses. "China's market has genuine demand for US agricultural products, but economic and trade cooperation has never been a one-way street," Huo Jianguo, former head of the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation under MOFCOM, told the Global Times. The US side should move in the same direction with China, take concrete steps on tariff relief, and continue to expand the scope of exemptions while reducing non-tariff barriers. As long as the two sides uphold reciprocal benefit and mutual respect, China-US economic and trade cooperation still has broad room to grow, Huo said. On the industry front, those expectations are already playing out on the exhibition floor. "It's our first time to attend the CIIE and it's been productive. We hope to take this platform as a stepping stone for building long-term relationships with our Chinese partners, bringing Amza products such as Toasted Flaxseed Butters and Purple Barley Bites to China's stores and e-commerce platforms," Jolma Ren, CEO of Oregon-based Amza Superfoods, told the Global Times on Friday. China is a very important market for US rice. For many years, the USA Rice Federation has been deeply engaged in promoting US rice in the Chinese market, and this year marks the fourth time that USA Rice has participated in the CIIE. USA Rice has long sought mutually beneficial partnerships with China's rice industry and hopes to offer Chinese consumers a wider variety of rice. This year, Mollie Buckler, Senior Director of Grower & International Relations at USA Rice, came to the CIIE with great enthusiasm, hoping to help the US rice industry establish connections with Chinese rice counterparts and continue to raise awareness of US rice in the Chinese market. "Trade is built on relationships, and CIIE gives us the chance to strengthen ours in person," Buckler told the Global Times on Friday. "USA Rice is committed to win-win cooperation with Chinese importers, processors, and retailers, and we're eager to explore how US rice can meet the needs of Chinese consumers." Chinese analysts said Chinese companies have always made purchasing decisions based on market demand, prices and commercial considerations. Amid changes in the US trade environment and tariff measures in recent years, many Chinese importers are also diversifying their suppliers. The US should work with China to advance reciprocal tariff reductions as reciprocal implementation of trade commitments is essential to creating stable conditions for bilateral agricultural trade, Chinese analysts said.

item.title: AI helps track tigers, gibbons and elephants to turn sightings into protection in China
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-06 23:21:00
A display showcases the AI-powered wildlife monitoring system used in Changchun, Northeast China's Jilin Province. Photo: Shan Jie/Global Times A wild Siberian tiger does not pose for an identification photograph. It may pass a forest camera sideways, turn its back or leave only its head in view. For a computer trying to establish which tiger has appeared, those incomplete glimpses present a challenge. Unlike human faces, the markings of endangered wild animals come with relatively few examples from which an algorithm can learn, Hu Xinyu, a senior manager at Jishi Media, which provides technical support for Northeast China Tiger and Leopard National Park's wildlife monitoring system, told the Global Times. Yet these brief encounters are becoming increasingly useful. At Northeast China Tiger and Leopard National Park, connected cameras and AI-assisted analysis help staff link an animal's appearance to its previous sightings, follow its movements and identify possible risks near villages. Across China, similar approaches are extending from forest images to rainforest sounds. The practical question is how to turn these records into knowledge that helps people protect wildlife. Recognizing the unseen The first task is getting information out of the forest. At Northeast China Tiger and Leopard National Park, a communications network operating in the 700 MHz frequency band connects cameras across mountainous terrain. Hu said footage can reach monitoring centers within about a minute of capture, allowing staff to examine activity without waiting for someone to retrieve a memory card. AI then helps sort the incoming material. But identifying a tiger in an image and deciding exactly which tiger it is are different tasks. According to Hu, the system's species recognition accuracy exceeds 90 percent, while individual identification accuracy for some species, including Siberian tigers and Amur leopards, exceeds 80 percent. Researchers still need to review uncertain matches. The distinction matters. Recognizing that a tiger has crossed a camera's field of view records its presence. Matching it to previous images allows researchers to assemble a history: where it travels, which areas it repeatedly visits and whether it appears with cubs. The park's monitoring platform associates identification numbers with images recorded at different locations. Stripes and spots provide distinguishing features, while repeated observations help staff trace dispersing youngsters and breeding families. For rare animals, however, collecting enough suitable examples remains difficult. An animal partly hidden by vegetation or photographed from an unfamiliar angle may offer few usable features. Hu said the team continues working with research institutions to improve identification. In Hainan's tropical rainforests, researchers have been examining another identifying feature: the voice. A gibbon moves through the forest in the Wuliang Mountains in Pu'er, Southwest China's Yunnan Province, on August 3, 2026. Photo: VCG Hainan gibbons spend much of their lives high in the trees, making direct observation difficult. Their calls offer a way to gather information when their bodies remain hidden. A study published in Scientia Silvae Sinicae in 2023 tested whether neural networks could distinguish male Hainan gibbons using spectrograms, visual representations of their calls. Working with recordings from seven males, researchers reported classification accuracy of 95.04 percent for the better-performing model. The result demonstrated a method for distinguishing those individuals. The example shows why wildlife monitoring requires methods adapted to each species. A camera may capture a tiger's markings; a recorder may capture a gibbon that cannot be seen. Both still depend on carefully collected and checked reference data. Experience with snow leopards also illustrates the continuing role of people. Researchers involved in a large-scale Sanjiangyuan survey described using AI to help remove empty camera images and classify animals. Identifying individual snow leopards still relied mainly on people comparing markings, with two observers checking their conclusions independently, according to the National Forestry and Grassland Administration. These systems reduce the burden of searching through records. But establishing what those records mean for a population requires further work, including field observations and ecological analysis. Turning data into protection Knowing where an animal has appeared can also help people decide where to avoid it. In Southwest China's Yunnan Province, Asian elephant monitoring combines infrared cameras, drones and AI image recognition to map elephant activity. It was reported that staff in Xishuangbanna were using these tools to produce activity heat maps, bringing observations from different locations together on a monitoring platform. The information becomes useful through the people and communication channels connected to it. Yunnan's forestry and grassland authorities told the Global Times in a previous interview that professional elephant protection teams carry out routine monitoring and issue warnings to nearby communities through WeChat, text messages and smart broadcasting systems, reminding residents to avoid elephants. AI is also being used to support the captive breeding of Yangtze finless porpoises. In Wuhan, Central China's Hubei Province, researchers have introduced an intelligent behavior monitoring system to follow interactions between mothers and calves, adding detailed observations to the work of animal carers. The system analyzes video to recognize several important mother-calf swimming positions and surfacing behavior. Researchers can use the resulting records to track nursing frequency and duration, assembling observations into standardized growth records for young porpoises. Bawangling National Nature Reserve in South China's Hainan Province provides a forest habitat for Hainan gibbons. Photo: VCG Previously, monitoring required staff to work around the clock in four shifts. Fatigue during overnight observation could affect data quality. The new system helps researchers organize observations more systematically and devote more time to breeding research. The application offers another route from images to conservation: repeated observations of how a calf swims and feeds become records that researchers can review, compare and use in caring for the animal. At the tiger and leopard park, staff similarly use monitoring information to warn communities when large predators approach settlements. Recent activity records also help rangers plan their routes, giving animals space while maintaining patrols. The forest images have another use beyond management. They provide material through which people far from wildlife habitats can learn about the animals living there. During a visit to Jishi Media in Changchun, Northeast China's Jilin Province, production staff described a familiar difficulty in wildlife filmmaking: a camera may record a remarkable moment without capturing enough material to explain an animal's wider life. A representative involved in ecological filmmaking told the Global Times that obtaining continuous footage of wild tigers, including feeding behavior, was difficult. The team draws on monitoring images and documentary materials, combining real footage with AI-generated sequences to present aspects of animal life that are hard to film. The approach is being explored in the documentary project Huxiao Gongsheng (Living with Tigers), which uses AI-generated content to visualize scenes beyond the reach of conventional filming. For the production team, AI offers a way to explain animal behavior that is difficult to capture continuously in the wild. The representative said real monitoring footage and documentary materials provide the basis for the storytelling, while generated sequences help illustrate feeding behavior and food-chain relationships. The team hopes this combination will help audiences understand both the animals' lives and the protection work surrounding them. Stories about tigers entering villages, for example, can also explain how wildlife-damage insurance compensates farmers for livestock losses, showing what coexistence involves for people living near their habitats. Back in the forest, the tiger may still give the camera only a fleeting view. The work continues after it has disappeared from the frame.

item.title: Yellow River Rejuvenated: Swans return, wetlands flourish and green dreams take root after 80 years of careful management
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-06 23:09:00
The Yellow River winds through the Jin-Shaan Grand Canyon between North China's Shanxi Province and Northwest China's Shaanxi Province. Photos on this page: VCG, IC As the weather turns chill, nature paints the Yellow River in vivid colors. Along its winding course, restored wetlands, green hills and golden farmlands form a changing landscape. In Sanmenxia, Central China's Henan Province, white swans return to spend the winter. Farther downstream, migratory birds gather in the wetlands of the Yellow River Delta in East China's Shandong Province. From the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau to the Bohai Sea, Yellow River, China's second-longest river, is witnessing an ecological transformation, as environmental restoration and green development reshape both its landscape and the lives of people along its banks. The changes come as China marks 80 years of Yellow River management. On Monday, the country stressed efforts to continuously improve protection and coordination to make the Yellow River even more beautiful. Solid efforts are called to be made to promote ecological protection and high-quality development in the Yellow River Basin. The Yellow River flows 5,464 kilometers through nine provinces and autonomous regions, crossing deserts and loess lands, before emptying into the Bohai Sea in Shandong. For centuries, the Yellow River was notorious for its devastating floods, frequent changes of course and heavy sediment loads. Decades of comprehensive management have significantly changed that picture. By 2025, the basin's soil and water conservation rate had reached 69.75 percent, with approximately 290,500 square kilometers of soil erosion areas initially brought under control. Additionally, the river's main stream had maintained Class II water quality for four consecutive years, reflecting continued improvements in the basin's ecological environment. The ecological benefits of a healthy Yellow River are also reaching areas beyond the river basin. At Daihai Lake in Ulaanqab, North China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, an ambitious water diversion project has helped replenish an inland lake that had long suffered from shrinking water levels. Wei Lei, deputy director of the Daihai Nature Reserve Service Center, told the Global Times during a recent interview that water from the Yellow River, approximately 160 kilometers away, is transported through three pumping stations. The project began supplying water in September 2022. Alongside ecological water replenishment, local authorities have promoted water-saving agriculture, restored wetland vegetation and reduced pollution. Some farmers have switched to less water-intensive crops, while others have found new income opportunities through tourism and related services. "Ecological restoration often depends on nature itself. What we can do is minimize human disturbance," Wei said. The changes at Daihai demonstrate how water conservation, ecological restoration and adjustments to local economic activities can work together to improve fragile environments. In Northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, the eastern foothills of the Helan Mountains offer another example of the economic opportunities created by greener development. Once dominated by barren land, the area has emerged as one of China's major wine-producing regions, with extensive vineyards replacing stretches of wasteland. The development of the wine industry has also stimulated tourism, hospitality and rural employment. In Haoyuan village, more than 75 percent of the local workforce is engaged in wine-related activities. Meanwhile, smart irrigation systems, agricultural waste recycling and other technologies are helping wineries improve resource efficiency and reduce their environmental footprint, according to the Xinhua News Agency. The Yellow River's development also has a digital dimension. The National Supercomputing Center in Jinan, Shandong Province, provides computing power for weather forecasting, climate prediction, industrial simulations and research into new materials and energy. The center has joined partners in 11 cities across the nine provincial-level regions along the river to establish a Yellow River Basin computing network alliance, enabling computing resources to be connected and shared. These digital "brains" are supporting scientific research and industrial innovation along the river. At the Yellow River's eastern end, agricultural innovation is breathing new life into saline-alkali land in Dongying, Shandong Province. Scientists and farmers have been developing salt-tolerant crop varieties and improving cultivation techniques to turn previously underused land into productive farmland, local media outlet sd.news.cn reported. In October, a newly developed corn variety grown on moderately to heavily saline-alkali land produced a yield of 656.24 kilograms per mu (1 mu equals 666.67 square meters), illustrating the potential of agricultural technology to improve productivity while making better use of challenging land resources. Beyond Dongying's farmland, the waters of the Yellow River also sustain wetlands vital to migratory birds. At the Shandong Yellow River Delta National Nature Reserve, the number of recorded bird species has risen from 187 when the reserve was established to 407. Millions of migratory birds stop here each migration season to rest and feed. Their arrival is also drawing visitors to the river's mouth. At dawn and dusk, flocks rise above the wetlands in shifting formations known as "bird waves," attracting birdwatchers and photographers from across China. Where the Yellow River completes its journey to the sea, these seasonal gatherings bring wildlife and new activity to its shores. The opening ceremony of the 2026 Gesar Cultural Tourism Festival takes place in the Yellow River headwaters region in Maqin county, Golog Tibetan autonomous prefecture, Northwest China's Qinghai Province, on August 4, 2026. Farmers harvest Hami melons at an agricultural cooperative in Zibo, East China's Shandong Province, on July 6, 2026. A technician inspects the server room at the Dongying Computing Center in the Dongying High-tech Industrial Development Zone, East China's Shandong Province. A photovoltaic power base beside the Yellow River glows under the setting sun in Cangtou town, Xin'an county, Luoyang, Central China's Henan Province. Migratory birds gather on exposed mudflats at Wuhai Lake after sediment flushed along the Yellow River lowers water levels in Wuhai, North China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, on September 23, 2026. Tourists ride a sheepskin raft on the Yellow River alongside rolling desert dunes in Shapotou, Zhongwei, Northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region.

item.title: Quad launches Malabar drills off Japan; expert says training fuels regional tensions as Japan risks overestimating own strength
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-06 21:09:00
Armed forces officers stand aboard a naval vessel at the Yokosuka base in Japan on November 5, 2026, as the US, Japan, India and Australia launch the Malabar 2026 joint maritime exercise. Photo: VCG Elements of armed forces from the US, Japan, India and Australia launched the Malabar 2026 maritime exercise on Thursday, with anti-submarine and anti-surface warfare drills scheduled in the Pacific Ocean south of Japan's Kanto region through November 12. Japan's Kyodo News claimed that the exercise aims to strengthen cooperation among the four members of the Quad security grouping with China in mind. According to the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force (JMSDF), participating units include Japan's JS Ise and JS Mogami, an attack submarine, and a P-1 maritime patrol aircraft. The US Navy is deploying an amphibious transport dock (LPD) and a P-8A patrol aircraft, while India is represented by the frigate INS Sahyadri. Australia is contributing the frigate HMAS Stuart from its Navy and a Royal Australian Air Force P-8A aircraft. The planned drills include anti-submarine warfare, anti-surface warfare and other tactical exercises. The JMSDF claimed the exercise was intended to improve its tactical capabilities and strengthen cooperation with the other participating forces, describing the drills as part of efforts to realize a "Free and Open Indo-Pacific." Song Zhongping, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Friday that anti-submarine warfare appears to be a key focus of the exercise, with the participating countries seeking to enhance their ability to conduct coordinated operations involving aircraft and surface vessels. Although the four countries have not explicitly identified China as a target, the location, participating equipment and training activities suggest that the drills appear to be aimed at Chinese submarine operations, as suggested by Japanese media, Song said. While such drills could enhance the four countries' joint anti-submarine capabilities, they also provide China with an opportunity to study their tactics and technologies, Song said. Chinese naval elements routinely conduct training beyond the island chains in the western Pacific, and China's military also has the capability to counter potential threats posed by such military activities, he added. India's Ministry of Defence claimed in a press release on Thursday that the exercise would enhance operational coordination, strengthen interoperability and facilitate exchanges of professional expertise through a series of engagements in harbor and at sea. Song said it looks like India has different strategic priorities from the other three countries, as its primary focus is on its interests in the Indian Ocean rather than the western Pacific or the South China Sea. By participating in the drills, India seeks to learn from the experience of the US, Japan and Australia and address shortcomings in its own equipment and operational capabilities. The Malabar drills began as a bilateral naval exercise between India and the US in 1992. Japan joined in 2015, while Australia returned to the exercise in 2020, bringing all four Quad countries into the drills, according to India's Ministry of Defence. Song warned that the Malabar drills should not be simply viewed as routine military exercises, as their combat-oriented nature would inevitably heighten tensions in the region. "Japan is seeking to use the multinational drills to deter China, but such an approach risks leading Tokyo into a serious strategic miscalculation by mistaking the combined military capabilities of the participating countries for Japan's own strength," Song noted. The Asia-Pacific is a high ground for peace and development. Those who follow the prevailing trend of peace can go far, while those who insist on stoking bloc confrontation find no support. Japan has courted and catered to countries outside the region to conduct so-called joint exercises, developed and deployed intermediate and long-range missiles, continuously beefed up military deployment in its southwestern islands, and accelerated remilitarization, becoming a real threat to regional security, Chinese Defense Ministry spokesperson Zhang Xiaogang said at a press conference on October 29. Chen Xi, another spokesperson for the ministry, on Friday said that Japan's reported plan to promote the defense industry as part of its economic policy is a smokescreen for accelerating its remilitarization. Chen said Japan's right-wing forces were reviving its military-industrial complex, pushing society toward war preparedness and the economy toward militarization, posing systemic risks to the Japanese people and global peace and stability. The spokesperson urged the international community to remain vigilant and prevent Japan from restarting its "war machine" and returning to the path of expansionism.

item.title: Pressuring for concessions? Europe should not misjudge China
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-06 19:57:00
China EU Photo:VCG Europe has increasingly adopted a dual-track approach in its economic and trade negotiations with China, talking while applying pressure. On the one hand, there is dialogue. In early October, the second meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism was held in Beijing, with the two sides reaching agreement on a list of 16 specific points of consensus. More recently, French President's Diplomatic Adviser Emmanuel Bonne, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, and Bernd Lange, Chair of the European Parliament's Committee on International Trade, have each led delegations to China. The European side has continued to signal its reluctance to engage in a trade war with China and its willingness to resolve trade and economic differences through dialogue and consultation. On the other hand, there is pressuring. At its autumn summit, the EU placed a proposed "kill switch" instrument, jointly put forward by France and Germany, high on its agenda. The mechanism would allow the bloc to shut its market to external parties when deemed necessary. The EU also intends to replicate its trade arrangement on Chinese hybrid vehicles in more sectors, including chemicals and machinery. Media reports have revealed that the bloc plans to impose further import caps or tariffs on Chinese products in which China has a competitive advantage, potentially as early as the first quarter of 2027. Meanwhile, calls within Europe for invoking the EU's "Anti-Coercion Instrument" (ACI) against China continue to grow louder. The EU's strategy brings to mind a rather telling image: One hand extends a business card across the negotiating table, while the other sharpens a knife underneath it. Brussels says it does not want a trade war, yet its toolbox of trade restrictions continues to expand. For the EU today, however, this is less a case of walking on two legs than of tripping over its own feet. The fundamental contradiction in its dual-track strategy stems from three major miscalculations. First, China will not accept pressure as a means of extracting concessions. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has repeatedly invoked the narrative that the EU's trade deficit with China reaches 1 billion euros ($1.12 billion) a day. Leaving aside the considerable distortions and one-sidedness in this figure, China has nevertheless taken full account of the difficulties facing Europe and reached pragmatic arrangements with the European side to address bilateral trade and economic differences, on the basis of equality and mutual benefit and in accordance with WTO rules. China's willingness to do so has absolutely nothing to do with any fear of the Franco-German "kill switch" or the EU's ACI. In fact, China has never yielded to a strategy of maximum pressure, as its economic and trade negotiations with the US have made abundantly clear. The Chinese government has also made its position explicit: Europe should not expect to extract benefits through pressure, nor should it underestimate China's resolve and ability to safeguard its own interests. The prerequisite for dialogue to produce substantive results is, ultimately, that both sides believe commitments made at the negotiating table are credible. The EU's practice of negotiating while applying pressure sends precisely the opposite signal: Agreements reached through dialogue do not necessarily constrain either side from taking unilateral action. If the outcomes of negotiations can be overturned at any moment, or subjected to additional conditions and renegotiated terms, what is the point of dialogue in the first place? As the EU's list of pressure tactics continues to grow while the outcomes of negotiations remain slow to materialize, mutual trust between China and Europe will gradually erode. This could well become the greatest risk facing their economic and trade relations in the years ahead. Second, the EU mistakes China's economic resilience for a vulnerability rooted in dependence on Europe. Some in Europe believe that China's insufficient domestic demand and alleged industrial overcapacity make it dependent on the European market. The facts and figures tell a very different story. Consumption has long been the main engine of China's economic growth, with domestic demand serving as a key pillar. In 2025, the contribution rate of final consumption expenditure to economic growth stood at 52 percent. China's total retail sales of consumer goods exceeded 50 trillion yuan ($7.15 trillion), making it the world's second-largest consumer market and the world's second-largest importer. In the first three quarters of 2026, domestic demand accounted for as much as 74.8 percent of China's economic growth. The picture is equally clear when it comes to industrial capacity. China's capacity utilization rate of industrial enterprises above the designated size nationwide was 74.4 percent in 2025, reflecting an overall balance between industrial supply and demand. The capacity utilization is even higher in high-tech manufacturing and strategic emerging industries. The temporarily lower capacity utilization in some traditional industries represents a localized and dynamic adjustment in the course of industrial upgrading, and is part of China's own strategic choice to foster new quality productive forces. If the European side assumes that China cannot sell its products and will therefore soften its position at the negotiating table, it is misjudging not only China's determination to defend its interests, but also the formidable resilience and confidence underpinning China's high-quality development. Third, expanding trade restrictions against China will ultimately backfire on Europe itself. Most of the Chinese products that the EU plans to subject to further import restrictions are intermediate goods essential to European industrial production. These high-quality, competitively priced products account for approximately half of China's total exports to Europe. At a time when energy prices and labor costs in Europe continue to rise, they play a crucial role in reducing production costs and enhancing the competitiveness of European exports. The EU regards its quota for China-EU hybrid vehicle trade as an example of successful pressure on China, and plans to replicate this approach in sectors such as chemicals and machinery. This wishful thinking overlooks a fundamental distinction: Automobiles are finished consumer goods, for which import quotas may indeed narrow trade imbalances in the short term. Chemicals and machinery, by contrast, are largely inputs for production and indispensable to the normal operation of European manufacturing. Economically speaking, simply copying and pasting the quota-based restrictions used for finished consumer goods into the intermediate goods sector makes little sense. If implemented, such measures would hit downstream industries across Europe first and hardest, pushing up their production costs and directly undermining the EU's own goal of protecting industrial competitiveness. Europe's own economic circumstances simply cannot sustain a strategy of applying pressure on China. Estimates by the European Central Bank and other institutions indicate that decoupling from China could add approximately 200 billion euros (approximately $224.4 billion) in costs annually. If Chinese suppliers were excluded from 10 key sectors, the EU could lose 840 billion euros ($942.4 billion) over the next five years. European politicians would do well to run these numbers for themselves. Recent large-scale protests in several European countries have largely reflected domestic concerns, including soaring energy prices, sluggish economic growth and inadequate public spending on people's livelihoods. These grievances share some underlying causes with what lies behind the so-called China-EU trade imbalance. Blaming China for Europe's problems is misguided to begin with; prescribing protectionism as the cure is even more misguided, amounting to a desperate attempt to treat the symptoms while ignoring the disease. China's position is equally clear: China is not the source of Europe's problems, but a partner in addressing them. The author is an international affairs observer. opinion@globaltimes.com.cn

item.title: China-developed airborne wind power system takes flight as developer explores AI computing aloft
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-06 19:52:00
Linyi Yunchuan's S4000 Stratosphere Airborne Wind Energy System (SAWES) rises to the sky in Yueyang, Central China's Hunan Province, on November 6, 2026. Photo: Tao Mingyang/GT Chinese energy technology company Linyi Yunchuan launched its S4000 Stratosphere Airborne Wind Energy System (SAWES) in Yueyang, Central China's Hunan Province, on Friday to test a new approach to supplying green electricity near cities. The firm's CEO told the Global Times that the company is also exploring the deployment of AI computing hardware on the airborne platform. At the launch site of around 0.033 hectare in Yueyang, the 67-meter-long structure, resembling a giant airship, rose steadily into the sky. Cables stretched between the airborne platform and the ground, anchoring the system while providing a channel for electricity generated aloft to reach users below, the Global Times observed. The demonstration focused on deployment under real operating conditions near a city, following the system's completion of a full flight verification at an altitude of 4,000 meters in Northwest China in August, according to the company. Beyond sending electricity to the ground, the company is experimenting with taking computing equipment closer to its power source. Dun Tianrui, CEO of Linyi Yunchuan, told the Global Times that the S4000 has space reserved for graphics processing units (GPUs), and that related experiment have already been conducted. "The S4000 already has enough space reserved for computing GPUs, and we have carried out related experiments," Dun said. He estimated that deploying GPUs on an airborne platform could cost less than $10 per kilogram, compared with about $10,000 per kilogram for deployment in space. The idea is to supply the hardware directly with wind-generated electricity while using cold air at high altitudes to reduce cooling requirements. Dun said mounting computing boards on the platform could also reduce the need for conventional buildings and cabinets used to house computing equipment. The experiments have also revealed engineering challenges. Dun said low temperatures had damaged some components used to suspend the computing equipment, highlighting the need to adapt the hardware to the proposed airborne computing system's operating environment. For electricity generation, the SAWES uses a helium-filled platform to lift lightweight generating equipment into the sky. Wind passes through a duct and drives turbines, while a tether anchors the platform and carries electricity to the ground, according to the company. The S4000 measures 67 meters long, 40 meters wide and 23 meters high, with an effective airborne payload exceeding one ton and a designed service life of 20 years. The company says the approach requires less land and faces fewer terrain constraints than conventional installations. However, the purpose of taking a generator into the sky is ultimately to deliver usable electricity, Dun said, explaining why the company is moving its demonstrations closer to consumers. "The generator itself is not the goal. Providing people with a stable electricity supply is the goal." Even if generation costs fall, electricity supply still involves spending on grid construction, dispatch and storage, the executive noted. Deploying airborne wind systems closer to users could help make better use of the technology, while making grid connection and public observation more convenient. Friday's launch follows a series of tests involving progressively larger operating heights. The previous-generation S500 model first flew to 500 meters in Jingmen, Central China's Hubei Province, in October 2024, completing an initial verification of the operating principle, according to the company. The S1000 reached 1,000 meters in the Poyang Lake area of Gongqingcheng, East China's Jiangxi Province, in January 2025. The S1500 completed a test flight in Hami, Northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, in September that year. In January 2026, the S2000 flew to 2,000 meters and completed a grid-connection test in Yibin, Southwest China's Sichuan Province. The S4000's August verification subsequently covered ascent, hovering, electricity-generation testing and recovery under high-altitude conditions, according to the company.

item.title: China 'isn't buying' Nvidia chips. Why are some Americans so rattled?
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-06 19:50:00
Nvidia H200 chip Photo: VCG Reuters recently cited "people familiar with the matter" as saying that about 600,000 Nvidia H200 chips piled up in Hong Kong awaiting shipment to the Chinese mainland because they have not been approved for release by the Chinese side. Although neither the Chinese government nor the US government nor Nvidia has confirmed the report, it has already sent some Americans into a tizzy. Some US think tank experts said they find it "bit of a puzzle" why China is being so cautious about Nvidia, while certain media outlets claimed that China is "restricting itself." Judging from the reactions of some people in the US, it seems they have forgotten who was the first to impose sanctions. In 2022, Washington imposed export controls on advanced chips destined for China under the pretext of "national security," immediately placing Nvidia's most advanced chips on the list of products banned from sale to China. These restrictions have since been tightened layer upon layer. Today, not only have affiliates and overseas subsidiaries of restricted Chinese companies been brought under the controls, but alternative routes for accessing advanced computing power through overseas cloud rental arrangements have also come under pressure. Some US politicians have even openly insisted that China must not be given any breathing room, arguing that even chips with reduced processing power should be kept out of its hands. So why is it that some Americans get rattled when China buys Nvidia chips, yet get equally rattled when China chooses not to buy them? Nvidia once held an overwhelmingly dominant position in China's AI chip market. However, successive rounds of US export controls have directly slashed its market share in China to around 30 percent of its previous level. Washington's decision to ease export licensing restrictions on H200 chips for China is essentially an attempt to find buyers for products that have already rolled off the production line but now lag two generations behind the most advanced chips. Yet the Chinese market has not rushed to buy them on the scale Washington anticipated. With large quantities of chips stuck in the distribution pipeline, inventory and revenue pressures are naturally mounting for the companies concerned. US institutions that had hoped to use sales of crippled versions of chips to China to help bankroll domestic semiconductor reshoring efforts are understandably finding it difficult to remain calm. There is a deeper strategic calculation behind this thinking among some in the US: By selling China relatively outdated chips, the US hopes to keep Chinese companies locked into the existing technology ecosystem, slow the development and iteration of China's homegrown chips, and preserve a stable technological gap between the two countries. They apparently assumed that a slight loosening of restrictions would trigger a buying spree in China. But the Chinese market today is no longer at a stage where it must buy whatever the US decides to make available. When procuring chips, companies must first consider long-term supply stability, the sustainability of technological roadmaps, and the security and controllability of supply chains. The actions taken by some in the US over the past several years have fundamentally changed the way Chinese companies make purchasing decisions. To expect them to disregard these risks and resume large-scale purchases is simply contrary to the most basic principles of commercial logic. Ultimately, it is not the Chinese market that is anxious now. The development of China's computing power industry in recent years has demonstrated that an independent technological path can provide sufficient computing capacity to sustain industrial growth. Rather than repeatedly urging China to buy American chips, some in the US would do well to acknowledge a basic reality: The global semiconductor landscape has changed. Any attempt to use export controls to lock other countries out of technological progress will ultimately come back to haunt those imposing the restrictions.

item.title: After 15 years of searching, Mauritian scholar's dream comes true
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 23:04:00
Seesaghur and Wu exchange gifts. Photo: Xinmin Evening News Hans Seesaghur, a scholar from Mauritius, had been looking for a Shanghai citizen named Wu Xinmin for 15 years. His dream finally came true. On November 2, Seesaghur and Wu Xinmin met face to face in Shanghai. In 2011, while pursuing his postgraduate studies at Wuhan University, Central China's Hubei Province, Seesaghur conducted research on the history of exchanges between China and Mauritius. During the process, Seesaghur, born in the 1980s, discovered that a Chinese table tennis delegation had visited Mauritius in 1972. In a news archive of the People's Daily, Seesaghur read Wu's name. However, despite years of searching, he was unable to contact Wu. In 2021, Seesaghur read an exclusive interview by the Xinmin Evening News with Wu. After contacting the media outlet, Seesaghur was able to meet Wu. Then, Wu was 23 years old and the captain of the Shanghai table tennis team. In 1972, Wu and Team China traveled to five African countries - Kenya, Ethiopia, Tanzania, Mauritius and Uganda - for a total of 68 friendly games. During their meeting, Wu shared with Seesaghur the materials of visiting itinerary, press clippings, and old photographs. Seesaghur is working on a book project, featuring the diplomatic history of Mauritius since its independence, with China-Mauritius relations serving as one of the key topics. Global Times
